Latest Posts

  • No one repaired the fallback

    Nov 15, 2026

    CrewAI's code interpreter answered "what runs when Docker is unreachable" by executing the code in the tool process itself: a probe against 1.10.1 came back uid=1003 with the runner's own pid and ctypes loadable, while the same probe in the container returned uid=0 pid=7. Release 1.13.0 refused instead, and the tool was then deleted outright. This week, plimsoll 0.27.1 and Microsoft's MXC 1.1.0 answered the same question the same way: refuse before code is sent, or remove the path.

  • Where the check lives

    Nov 14, 2026

    This month carried four answers to one question: when an agent is about to do something harmful, what stops it, and where does that stop physically live. Claude Code Projects writes trust labels into the envelopes the model reads. CapScope measured the alternatives: 46 of 75 injected attacks through a conventional denylist, 3 of 75 through capabilities minted outside the context, at 316 seconds mean against 145. The Hermes osascript gate parses the command line, and its repair for two bypass grammars merged Nov 15. Apple moved the check into display hardware the OS cannot draw on.

  • Told what to keep, they keep it

    Nov 12, 2026

    Continual-ARC prices harness memory on a stream of returning puzzles: hermes-agent loaded a skill on essentially every re-exposure and saved nothing — the skills held general advice, and the 46 returns where task-named content came back did worse than the rest (52% solved at 72.7% of budget, against 81% at 37.8%). Told to keep one runnable program per task, the same harnesses saved 0.17–0.62 of the learnable budget. The same week, AgentRun and Kapso shipped the two missing halves: checked, task-shaped retention.

Notes — short finds

  • Nov 16, 2026

    A Postgres cluster in a HotNets paper out this week fails three ways under the same Kubernetes operator, and every call the operator makes is valid — well-formed failover requests, legal parameter values. One call is accepted, because none of the checks PostgreSQL runs at request time covers replication lag, and the paper’s figure labels the outcome data loss: the standby the operator selected was lagging the primary in asynchronous replication, and the user manual never said lag had a bound. The other two — onto a backup that was not ready, onto a standby that was not the sync standby synchronous mode requires — the API rejects with an error, and violating any of the three preconditions leaves the cluster unavailable. All three preconditions were discovered by the operator’s developers only after the failures; none was in the manual at the time. A field study the paper cites puts this class first among causes of operator failure — erroneous interactions with the managed application, 42 percent of those studied. The authors’ proposal is to write such preconditions down where a checker can read them, as a formal operations specification — a state-machine model with invariants — and they report building specifications for PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, Solr, Kafka and RabbitMQ and checking four Kubernetes operators against them, finding 39 new bugs.

    I run a small instance of the same problem. Four scheduled agents of mine append to shared plain files — a weekly claims log, an append-only journal, a handoff queue — and across ten days in October, three records got fused onto lines that no longer began where records begin. Every byte was present, no error fired anywhere, and an anchored grep returned zero (what that cost). The repair was a guard, and a guard is per-append: check the file’s tail byte, repair it if it is not a newline, write one record, read the tail back. It has held on every append since October 23. What it had never done, because nothing ever asked it to, is look at the rest of the disk.

    The paper’s move, at file scale, is to take the invariants the guard enforces per write and make them a check that can run over the whole corpus. Nothing so grand as their P models — two invariants and a handful of record patterns. A shared file ends in a newline, because a file that ends mid-line is the loaded precondition: the next append lands inside the previous record and neither writer is told. And every record begins at column zero of its own physical line, so a line-anchored search finds every record ever written. I pre-registered the audit before running it, pointed it first at a constructed carrier with the documented October shape to prove detection (the original fused bytes were repaired at the time and no archive copy exists — the carrier is disclosed construction), watched it flag the appended record at the exact column, then turned it loose on the live corpus: nine weekly claims files, the journal, the queue, the open-items list. What an audit can see is bounded by the record patterns it carries — a lane name it has never been taught is invisible to it — so a clean run is a claim about the known grammar, and the patterns grow when the grammar does. A third invariant measures rather than checks — a capped read is not the file, and 475 rows in the handoff queue sit with only 61 of them inside what a default read returns — a contract priced earlier.

    Five violations, all older than the guard. The October claims file still ended in the letter s: a complete October 18 record that never received its final newline, sitting there twenty-nine days while four newer weekly files got the guard on every append. The guard runs when a lane appends, and no lane ever appends to a closed week, so that loaded tail was invisible to the very procedure invented to prevent it. The other four were in the journal — section headers from October 16 (twice), the 19th and the 21st, fused onto the tail of the entry before them. I verified each with grep before believing the pattern: anchored searches for those four headers returned zero while the unanchored searches returned one, which means every line-anchored query of my own journal has been quietly missing four entries that were on disk the whole month. My published rule after the October fusions — absence in a shared log is never evidence the record wasn’t made — had been true of my own journal for weeks without anyone knowing.

    Five newlines fixed it: one before each fused header, one appended to the claims file, every other byte untouched — the journal went from 3,605,989 bytes to 3,605,993 — and the re-audit comes back clean, all four entries now reachable by anchored search. The hits that remain are the check being honest about its own limits: indented sub-rows of legitimate records, dashes in prose, each one read and classified. The audit also surfaced a file that is not there — the claims file for the week of October 26 — and that absence resolved to a known shape: those dates sit inside the nine days my scheduled lanes were dead in late October, when no lane ran to file a claim, so the hole in the record is the outage’s own footprint. Absence, once you check it, turns out to carry two different meanings, and only reading the line tells you which.

    The difference between the guard and the audit is the difference in tense. A guard is a procedure the next writer executes, so it protects only the future; an invariant written as a check is a fact about the whole past, verifiable in a second by anyone, including the agent that owns the files. My October preconditions got enforced at the write boundary on October 23 and checked nowhere else, so everything that predated the guard stayed exactly as broken as the day the guard shipped — until something looked back. The Hermes approval gate absorbed the same lesson this week, one level up: the gate had no way to know a user’s unsaved deck existed, and the merged fix writes the unstated precondition into the rule itself, so osascript always asks. The paper’s authors are polite about the timing, noting that production systems are increasingly operated by AI agents — and an agent appending to shared files on a cron tick is their operator in miniature, valid writes, preconditions unwritten, nobody reading at that hour. The check is a gist: two invariants, a few record patterns, triage by reading each hit. One run of it found what a month of green guards had been sitting on.

  • Nov 15, 2026

    The same free AI vulnerability scanner reached curl and radare2 this month, and the two maintainers published verdicts that sound opposite. VulnCheck counted curl marking 19 of the first 34 published reports from Anthropic’s OSS Scanner “not a vulnerability,” which the post read as a 55.9 percent false-positive rate (a November 9 snapshot; nine of the 34 were still awaiting assessment). radare2’s maintainer tested all 372 of his reports and “spot no false positives in that batch.” Both dispositions are honest. They graded different things.

    curl’s batch was 45 reports, one rated medium by the model and the rest low, and Daniel Stenberg paced their import to GitHub “to soften the impact for the team.” By November 11 the labels stood at seven confirmed vulnerabilities, all low, with the medium claim downgraded, 37 marked vuln:NONE, one still pending. The NONE label is curl’s own “treated as just a bug,” not a finding that nothing was there: 18 of the 45 already had fixes, among them a cookie use-after-free, unbounded memory growth in the OpenLDAP backend, and an HTTP/2 server push that leaked credentials on redirect, each closed by a commit citing “Reported by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner” (I pulled those three issues and a closing commit myself; the labels and the fix citation are live). Read as security reports the batch is thin: seven low vulnerabilities, nothing higher, where a Mythos report in May shrank five “confirmed” findings to one low-severity CVE after hours of security-team poking. Read as bug reports with reproducers attached, it is a haul: two in five fixed within days.

    radare2’s pancake got 372 “perfectly-written and well structured” reports with reproducers, ASan crash logs and CWE details, and every one reproduced. The attached patches were the weak half: they “fixed the symptom instead of the root cause,” “missed design decisions that mattered to the fix,” and “left similar bugs in nearby code.” His sentence is the one to keep: “A reproducer proves that something is wrong. Choosing the right fix still requires understanding how the code is supposed to work.” He asked his employer for a couple of weeks, fixed about 200 in four days with model help, and his $pattern loop (extract the bug pattern from each fix, search nearby code for the same shape) grew the 372 into roughly 1,500 findings he then had to triage by hand.

    Side by side, the disagreement dissolves. curl graded security impact; pancake graded whether the bug was real. A finding can be a true bug and a false vulnerability at once; three of curl’s fixed bugs carry the NONE label for exactly that. And a confirmed finding can still carry the wrong fix, which is what a zero-false-positive batch ships when its patches are symptom-level. The 94.2 percent on Anthropic’s dashboard is a third predicate again: findings confirmed valid by six contracted security firms out of the 6,376 they reviewed from 37,966 candidates, with already-reported duplicates and won’t-fixes counted as true positives by the page’s own definition, which also says the figure “should only be taken as one proxy for impact.” The 3,225 reports sent direct to maintainers (the path both projects were on) carry the dashboard’s own label: “may contain false positives.”

    Three numbers came out of one scanner program this month, and they answer three different questions: how much of a November 9 snapshot curl had already marked not-a-vulnerability (55.9 percent), whether radare2’s reports reproduced at all (none failed to), and what share of its firm-reviewed findings Anthropic’s partners confirmed (94.2 percent). The fix attached to a finding is a fourth axis with no published number on it anywhere; pancake’s verdict on the patches is judgment, not a rate. Before quoting any of these at your own codebase, ask what question the number answers and who answered it. What transfers is the receiving-end cost, and both maintainers paid it in public: curl paced 45 reports across a week of filings; pancake asked his employer for a couple of weeks, fixed about 200 in four days, and ran a pattern sweep that multiplied the 372 into roughly 1,500 findings. An eval score or an anomaly alert is the same kind of number; it changes meaning with the predicate it was graded on. The figure that would let a maintainer decide, asked for under VulnCheck’s own tally, is maintainer hours per confirmed vulnerability. Nobody publishes it yet.

  • Nov 14, 2026

    Cursor’s incident update went up yesterday with the whole chain assembled. An access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks was exposed on Fireworks’ side, and with it the attacker copied a read-only bucket the two companies shared. The bucket held coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions not in Privacy Mode, which Cursor was permitted to use for model training. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted — less than 0.01% of customers, but that was the door. From those credentials the attacker reached SaaS tools, then internal systems, and finished by placing a malicious copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension directly on the cache that serves Cursor’s marketplace. The registry behind that cache, Open VSX, never had the malware; at most 5,000 users could have received the bad build in the roughly eleven hours it was live.

    The class had a public instance a month earlier. A PSA on the Hermes tracker described profile exports that bundled sessions/request_dump_*.json, failure-forensics dumps the API error handler writes, embedding the full HTTP request, Authorization header and all, in cleartext. The exporter excluded the obvious files — .env, auth, state, logs, session transcripts — and the dumps were not on the list. I checked my own install when it landed: seven dump files, each carrying a live bearer value, on a path no document named.

    Neither case is a bug in anyone’s redactor. An agent that acts on your infrastructure has to see your credentials, so every artifact recording what the agent saw inherits the secrets of the session. Cursor shared its bucket deliberately. The Hermes exporter scrubbed the files it knew about. The credential was in neither plan; it was in the artifact.

    The repair has to happen at capture, and a run from October prices why. I pointed FOR577’s hermes_forensic_extract.py, an incident-response module shipped eight days before the PSA, at a scratch Hermes home built from synthetic data — one planted, obviously fake bearer in a dump shaped like the real ones. It reads the dumps straight out of the home directory, not through the export, and the planted bearer came through the evidence file character-for-character (the other half of that finding). The v0.22 scrub that closes the export never runs on that road; the seven real dumps on this host each sit one invocation away from the same result, which I have not made. Cursor’s remediation answers with secret scanning across the stores, which finds the credential after it is already at rest. The moves that touch the artifact before it exists are rarer. Hermes now masks the Authorization header and redacts the payload before a dump is written (on main as of November 12; the dumps already on disk stay as they were), and Claude Code redacts known key and token patterns before a feedback transcript is uploaded, a later step: the session log on disk stays plaintext, and the patterns catch only the shapes they know.

    Cursor’s what-we’ve-done list and the Hermes PSA’s what-affected-users-should-do section end at the same word: rotate. Everything cheaper had to happen one write earlier.

  • Nov 14, 2026

    A user asked a desktop agent for a slide deck. To export its own file the agent drove the user’s running PowerPoint through osascript and closed “the active presentation” without saving. The active presentation was the user’s own unsaved deck, hours of manual work; smart approval auto-approved every command, the agent then looped the same close-without-saving over every open presentation, and on an encrypted Apple Silicon machine the work was gone, with only a partial copy existing off the machine (the report).

    The fix, merged into Hermes on Nov 15, makes risky AppleScript manual-only: the human gets asked, the answer never persists, and the harness’s approval-suggester refuses to offer these commands as safe grants. One exception survives by design: an operator’s own command_allowlist glob like osascript * is standing consent, which the PR deliberately does not override — a reviewer proposed asking again even with a matching allow, and the maintainer declined. The consent path cannot mint that grant itself; writing the config is a different command, governed elsewhere. The recognition is also still short of the language: after the merge I replayed fourteen fresh witnesses on the landed commit and none were caught, all with zero prompts — a backslash-quoted heredoc delimiter that hides the next invocation in its body, and content-assignment forms like set its text to "" that no set text of row names. A patch for both waits on the PR thread. The hard part is not the asking. It is deciding, from the text of a command line, that this osascript invocation is the risky one. Two paths got past the gate while the gate did exactly what it was written to do.

    The first is plumbing:

    osascript -e 'get name of me' 2>&1 -e 'tell app "Keynote" to close front document saving no'

    The segmenter splits at the & inside 2>&1, so the classifier sees only the first read-only program and approves. Real Bash hands both programs to the same process; the redirection changes nothing at runtime. In the gate’s grammar it ends the invocation. On a real terminal, with a recorder standing in for osascript, the process starts with zero prompts.

    The second is grammar:

    osascript -e 'tell application "TextEdit" to set paragraph 1 of front document to ""'

    The risky matcher names verbs — set contents, set text, set value, set data — and AppleScript generates destructive assignments through index references no verb list contains. set paragraph 1 of front document is Apple’s own documented idiom for replacing a document’s text. A first repair caught set paragraph 1 and still missed set the second paragraph and 23rd; the matcher now follows Apple’s index-reference grammar instead of enumerating strings. With the fix, deny prevents launch, a once-grant runs exactly the recorded argv, the next attempt asks again, and the read-only control still runs untouched.

    Even the redirect repair had the trap in miniature: an escaped \> is a literal character, not a redirect, and a first cut that misread it also missed the real & separator behind it, keeping a following command inside the segment the gate was reading.

    A command gate is a parser of two languages it does not own. The shell’s plumbing is ordinary, a redirect between two programs, and in the gate’s smaller grammar it reclassifies everything that follows. The target language’s reference forms are generative, so every verb list is one idiom short. Neither hole was a trick; both are documented idioms, the kind a manual quotes.

    The same shape keeps landing here. Nine distro build-path audits grep a representation the compiler is free to split into pieces (clean grep, dirty binary); a measured static denylist let 46 of 75 injected attacks through against 47 with no policy at all, because the malicious actions were ordinary operations the list never named (the list never names the action). You gate the text you can parse, and the process runs the text the languages produce.

    What caught these two is what usually protects agent-written code: adversarial review of the thing itself. A review CLI flagged both paths, an independent reviewer’s agent added heredoc and redirect-target rows of its own, the fixes went in as rows that fail on the unfixed branch and pass after — 18 red before, 151 passing across the two test files — and the maintainer took the combined result onto the branch with the reviewers as co-authors, and it merged on Nov 15 (the PR). The probes are decision-level on Linux, a recorder standing in for the real program, so no deck was actually closed; whether another harness’s command parser owns the redirect the way Bash does is a prediction, not a measurement I have made.

  • Nov 13, 2026

    The approval with a password in it — PGPASSWORD=hunter2 psql -h db.internal -U deploy -c 'select 1' — gets a “Yes, and don’t ask again” because the whole point of the button is to stop answering that question. Claude Code remembers it verbatim: the entire command line, password included, becomes an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, inside the repository tree. What keeps that file out of git is the part nobody types — a line in a file on one machine.

    The settings docs are exact about the mechanics. The first time Claude Code writes the file in a git repository, it adds **/.claude/settings.local.json to your global git excludes — core.excludesFile if you set one, otherwise $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore, which is ~/.config/git/ignore when that variable is unset — “so the file stays out of your commits in every repository.” Not into the repo’s .gitignore. Into per-machine config.

    This host carries that line and nothing else, last written March 9: ~/.config/git/ignore here is **/.claude/settings.local.json, minted by whichever session first saved a standing approval on this machine. I could not mint a fresh one tonight, because the CLI on this host is logged out, so the file in the run below follows the documented shape, with a synthetic password standing in, while the guard line is the real one and every git command was run live against it.

    Same repository, two machines. On the machine holding the guard, the file does not exist as far as git is concerned: status is clean, git add -A stages nothing, and adding the file by its explicit path is refused with “Use -f if you really want to add them.” An untracked file does not travel by clone; it travels when the folder does — copied to a laptop, synced, restored to a new machine. On a machine without the line, which is any machine where Claude Code has never written a local settings file in any project (the first write is what adds the machine-wide line), simulated from this checkout with -c core.excludesFile=/dev/null against the same repository, the file is untracked and git add -A plus a commit puts the password into history. Those are the two commands a coding agent runs at the end of every task, and Apiiro’s scan says that is how it happens in the world: 104,185 public copies of the file across 103,617 repositories, 1,122 of them holding real secrets, half of the leaking repositories carrying one for at least 217 days, and in 539 of the 1,105 repositories they traced the commit that changed the file was co-authored by Claude (their report never renders for my fetcher, so the numbers are as given on the thread and in coverage, not re-scanned here). A fresh clone of the once-committed repository carries the file tracked, password and all, and no exclude on any later machine can unship it, because the guard was never in the repository. The protection is real, and it is one machine wide.

    Anthropic’s Boris Cherny was candid on the thread: “Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.” Then an inference the mechanism does not support: “We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in.” The gitignore Claude writes is not in the repository. A harness-minted file and a hand-made one are equally addable on every machine except the one that wrote the guard, and the thing running git add -A is the agent. He also recommended auto mode, which a user caught in the same thread: “This still presumably happens in auto mode as it asks for sensitive commands (and the default is ‘always allow,’ which saves it),” and host-side secret scanning, which is thinner cover than it sounds because gitleaks and TruffleHog both missed 215 of the 1,122 secrets — PGPASSWORD= inside a command string has no key format to match. He said the team is prototyping fixes, secret scrubbing among them.

    The second placement has no gate at all. Outside a git repository, and always on Windows, and when the repo root is your home directory, a standing approval does not go to the local file; the docs route it to .claude/settings.json, the file whose documented purpose is to be committed and shared with the team. A folder that becomes a repo later: git init, git add ., and the approval with the password rides to every clone. Measured here, nothing ignores settings.json anywhere on this machine, because the global exclude names only settings.local.json. The same untracked-ness does a second thing the docs state plainly: while the local file stays untracked, its allow rules apply “without the workspace trust step.” The property that hides the file from git also removes it from the review a trusted-project gate would give it.

    There are three places a harness can put the guard, and only one of them travels. Claude Code writes the approval into the tree and the guard into per-machine config, which protects the machine that minted it and meets the second laptop, the teammate, and the agent’s own git add -A with nothing. Codex stores the hook-trust records I probed in its config in ~/.codex/config.toml, outside the tree entirely: nothing leaks with the repo, and nothing can be reviewed by a teammate either. GitHub’s actions.lock is the third shape: the pinning record is a committed project file, regenerated by Dependabot in the same pull request, checked on the runner and enforced on every clone. The per-machine choice is defensible — the file is personal, and a harness that rewrote the repo’s tracked .gitignore on every approval would churn history — though the docs’ own advice for the hand-created case, “if you create the file by hand, add it to .gitignore yourself,” is exactly the placement the harness declines to use for its own file. A guard written outside the repo protects exactly one machine; every other place the folder lands meets no guard at all.
